Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the $lang translation.
5. The target language is $lang.

Due to the power of discriminatory conditioning of self and dharmas,
they manifest semblances of self and dharmas.
grasp these as real self and dharmas.
through the power of dream affliction,
the mind appears as various external objective forms.
During the dream, they grasp them as truly existing external objects.
Only upon waking do they realize they are merely transformations of the dream.
This body of ours and the external world
They are only transformations of consciousness.
Due to delusion, one grasps at a self and various objects.
Once awakened to the fundamental absence of self and dharmas,
Then, relying on the wisdom of these two emptinesses,
one cultivates the contemplation of consciousness-only,
and practices such as the six pāramitās and four means of attraction.
Gradually subduing and severing the two hindrances of afflictions and knowable objects,
one realizes the thusness revealed by the two emptinesses.
When the ten stages are perfected,
the eight consciousnesses transform into the four wisdoms of bodhi.
When obscurations to thusness are exhausted,
one accomplishes the dharmadhātu body, the fruit of great nirvāṇa.
This third approach uses consciousness to refute objects,
aligning with the Chán school's principle of ceasing false thoughts to cultivate the mind.
Since it is known that external objects are empty,
one does not cultivate external phenomena and activities,
but only ceases falsity and cultivates the mind.

The Mind Suchness Gate has ten names.
First, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha Gate,
because it is free from confusion.
Second, it is called the Non-dual Equality Gate,
Third, it is called the One Path of Purity Gate,
because it has no diverging forks.
Fourth, it is called the Non-arising and Immovable Gate,
because it is devoid of karmic activity.
Fifth, it is called the Uninterrupted and Unbound Gate,
because there is nothing to eliminate or obstruct.
Sixth, it is called the Neither Coming Nor Going Gate,
because it has no above or below.
Seventh, it is called the Transcendental World Gate,
because it is free from the four characteristics.
Eighth, it is called the Extinction and Quiescence Gate,
because it has no going or direction.
Ninth, it is called the Great Universal Characteristic Gate,
because it has no particular characteristics.
Tenth, it is called the Suchness Gate,
because it is free from falsity.

The Birth-and-Death Gate has ten names.

because it conceals the Tathāgata's Dharma Body.
